items.title: Unsound Reasoning Attention Opens: Sixteen Doctrines Named

items.zh: 復次，云何不如理作意施設建立？嗢拕南曰：執因中有果、顯了、有去來、我、常、宿作因、自在等、害法、邊無邊、矯亂、計無因、斷、空、最勝、淨、吉祥，由十六異論。
items.en: Further, how is the establishment of unsound reasoning attention to be understood? A summary verse states: holding that effect exists within cause, manifestation, past and future truly existing, self, permanence, prior deeds as cause, sovereign lordship and the rest, harming as the true Dharma, having or lacking limits, evasive equivocation, positing no cause, annihilation, and emptiness, supremacy, purity, and auspiciousness — through sixteen divergent doctrines.

items.zh: 由十六種異論差別，顯不如理作意應知。何等十六？一、因中有果論，二、從緣顯了論，三、去來實有論，四、計我論，五、計常論，六、宿作因論，七、計自在等為作者論，八、害為正法論，九、有邊無邊論，十、不死矯亂論，十一、無因見論，十二、斷見論，十三、空見論，十四、妄計最勝論，十五、妄計清淨論，十六、妄計吉祥論。
items.en: It should be understood that unsound reasoning attention is made manifest through these sixteen distinct divergent doctrines. What are the sixteen? First, the doctrine that effect exists within cause; second, the doctrine of manifestation through condition; third, the doctrine that past and future truly exist; fourth, the doctrine positing a self; fifth, the doctrine positing permanence; sixth, the doctrine of prior deeds as cause; seventh, the doctrine positing sovereign lordship and the like as creator; eighth, the doctrine that harming is the true Dharma; ninth, the doctrine of having or lacking limits; tenth, the doctrine of evasive equivocation about the deathless; eleventh, the doctrine positing no cause; twelfth, the doctrine of annihilation; thirteenth, the doctrine of emptiness; fourteenth, the doctrine of false supremacy; fifteenth, the doctrine of false purity; sixteenth, the doctrine of false auspiciousness.

items.title: The First Doctrine in Full: Why the Vārṣagaṇya School Held That Effect Exists Within Cause

items.zh: 因中有果論者，謂如有一若沙門、若婆羅門，起如是見，立如是論：常常時、恒恒時、於諸因中具有果性。謂雨眾外道作如是計。
items.en: The doctrine that effect exists within cause: there are certain renunciants or brahmins who hold such a view and establish such a doctrine — that always, at every time without exception, effect exists as a property already within its cause. It is the Vārṣagaṇya school of non-Buddhist teachers that holds this position.

items.zh: 問：何因緣故，彼諸外道起如是見，立如是論，顯示因中具有果性？答：由教及理故。教者，謂彼先師所造教藏，隨聞轉授傳至于今，顯示因中先有果性。理者，謂即如彼沙門、若婆羅門，為性尋思，為性觀察，住尋思地，住自辦地，住異生地，住隨思惟觀察行地。
items.en: Question: For what reason do those non-Buddhist teachers hold this view and establish this doctrine, declaring that the effect already exists within the cause? Answer: Because of scripture and reasoning. Scripture means the body of teachings composed by their former masters, handed down by hearing and passed on to the present day, which declares that the effect exists beforehand within the cause. Reasoning means that some śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa, a speculator by nature and an examiner by nature, stands on the ground of speculation, on the ground of his own devising, on the ground of an ordinary being, on the ground of examining by following his own thinking.

items.zh: 彼作是思：若從彼性此性得生，一切世間共知、共立彼為此因；非餘。又求果者，唯取此因，非餘。又即於彼，加功營搆諸所求事，非餘。又若彼果，即從彼生，不從餘生。是故彼果因中已有。
items.en: They reason thus: if this effect-nature arises from that cause-nature, the whole world alike recognises and establishes that cause-nature, and no other, as the cause of this effect. Further, one who seeks a given effect takes up only this cause, and no other. Further, it is on that very cause that effort and labour are actually applied in pursuit of the desired outcome, and on no other. Further, that effect arises specifically from that cause, and from no other. Therefore, that effect must already exist within its cause.

items.zh: 若不爾者，應立一切是一切因，為求一果應取一切，應於一切加功營搆，應從一切一切果生。如是由施設故，求取故，所作決定故，生故，彼見因中常有果性。
items.en: Were it otherwise, then anything at all should be the cause of anything at all; seeking a single effect should require taking up every possible cause; effort should have to be applied to everything without distinction; and any effect at all should arise from anything at all. It is thus through convention, through seeking, through the fixed determinacy of effort, and through arising itself, that they hold effect to exist perpetually within cause.

items.title: The Refutation: A Cause Only Ever Needs a Condition to Produce Its Effect

items.zh: 應審問彼：汝何所欲？何者因相？何者果相？因果兩相為異不異？若無異相，便無因果二種決定。因果二種無差別故，因中有果，不應道理。
items.en: One should press them with this question: what, precisely, do you mean? What is the mark of a cause? What is the mark of an effect? Are these two marks, cause and effect, different from each other or not different? If they are not different, then there can be no fixed distinction between the two at all — cause and effect being simply identical, it makes no sense to speak of "effect existing within cause."

items.zh: 若有異相，汝意云何？因中果性為未生相？為已生相？若未生相，便於因中果猶未生，而說是有，不應道理。若已生相，即果體已生，復從因生，不應道理。是故因中非先有果；然要有因，待緣果生。
items.en: If they are different, then consider this: is the effect-nature within the cause already-arisen, or not-yet-arisen? If not-yet-arisen, then the effect has, within the cause, not yet come to be at all — to call it "existing" makes no sense. If already-arisen, then the effect's own substance has already come to be, and to then say it "arises again from the cause" equally makes no sense. Therefore, effect does not pre-exist within cause. Rather, there must be a cause, and, given a further condition, the effect then arises.

items.title: Five Tests for Whether One Existing Thing Truly Contains Another, and the First Doctrine Closes

items.zh: 又有相法於有相法中，由五種相方可了知。一、於處所可得，如甕中水。二、於所依可得，如眼中眼識。三、即由自相可得，如因自體，不由比度。四、即由自作業可得。五、由因變異故，果成變異；或由緣變異故，果成變異。
items.en: Further, whenever one existing thing genuinely exists within another existing thing, this can be known through five marks. First, it can be found occupying a location, as water is found within a jar. Second, it can be found within its proper support, as eye-consciousness is found within the eye. Third, it can be found through its own characteristic, as a cause's own substance is found — not through mere inference. Fourth, it can be found through its own distinct function. Fifth, when the cause undergoes change, the effect correspondingly changes; or when the condition undergoes change, the effect correspondingly changes.

items.zh: 是故彼說常常時、恒恒時，因中有果，不應道理。由此因緣，彼所立論非如理說。
items.en: It is for this reason that their claim — that effect exists within cause always, at every time without exception — does not accord with reason. For this reason, the doctrine they establish is not a soundly reasoned teaching.

items.zh: 如是不異相故，異相故，未生相故，已生相故，不應道理。
items.en: Thus, because of the aspect of non-difference, the aspect of difference, the aspect of the not-yet-arisen, and the aspect of the already-arisen, it does not accord with reason.

items.title: The Second Doctrine: Effects Are Manifested by Conditions, Not Produced by Them

items.zh: 從緣顯了論者，謂如有一，若沙門、若婆羅門，起如是見，立如是論：一切諸法，性本是有，從眾緣顯，不從緣生。謂即因中有果論者及聲相論者作如是計。
items.en: The doctrine of manifestation through condition: there are certain renunciants or brahmins who hold such a view and establish such a doctrine — that the nature of every phenomenon fundamentally already exists, and is merely made manifest by an assembly of conditions, rather than actually produced by them. It is the very same holders of the doctrine that effect exists within cause, together with the Sound-nature theorists, who hold this position.

items.zh: 問：何因緣故，因中有果論者見諸因中先有果性從緣顯耶？答：由教及理故。教如前說。理者，謂如有一，為性尋思，為性觀察，廣說如前。
items.en: Question: For what reason do those who hold that the effect exists within the cause see the effect, already existing within the causes, as made manifest by conditions? Answer: Because of scripture and reasoning. Scripture is as explained before. Reasoning means that someone is a speculator by nature and an examiner by nature, as explained at length before.

items.zh: 彼如是思：果先是有，復從因生，不應道理。然非不用功為成於果。彼復何緣而作功用？豈非唯為顯了果耶？彼作如是妄分別已，立顯了論。
items.en: They reason thus: if an effect already exists beforehand, then to say it again "arises from" a cause makes no sense. Yet it is not the case that no effort at all is needed to bring about the effect — so for what reason, then, is effort actually exerted? Is it not solely in order to make the effect manifest? Having reasoned in this mistaken way, they establish the doctrine of manifestation.

blocks.text: Fascicle 6 turns to the fourth gateway of the three grounds of thought: **unsound reasoning attention** (不如理作意), shown through **sixteen divergent doctrines** (十六種異論). These are philosophical positions held by non-Buddhist thinkers, and two of them by some Buddhist schools. Each is presented in the same way: the doctrine, who holds it, their reasons from scripture and reasoning, and the refutation. Venerable Miào Jìng's advice: the "renunciants and brahmins" here are, in today's terms, philosophers. Read the arguments as philosophy.

Several passages are missing from Ru-Yi's translation (now supplied in our own translation, marked as ours), mostly the formal questions "Why do these outsiders hold this view? Answer: through scripture and reasoning …" that open each argument (0303c11–c16, 0304a16–a19), and a summary sentence (0304a11).

The sixteen: effect exists in the cause; effects are manifested by conditions; past and future truly exist; a self; permanence; prior causes (fatalism); a creator god; harm as righteousness; finitude and infinity; evasive equivocation; no cause; annihilation; denial of everything; supremacy of one's own caste; purity by ritual; and false auspiciousness. Fascicle 6 covers the first five.

Master Cháng Bǎi: though there were ninety-five or ninety-six non-Buddhist schools, "they reduce to sixty-two views, and their gist never exceeds the sixteen". He adds that two of the sixteen are held within Buddhism too: the reality of past and future (the Sarvāstivāda) and a kind of self (the Vātsīputrīya's person "neither identical to nor apart from the aggregates").

subs.head: Effect already exists in the cause

blocks.text: The first doctrine: "effect exists as a property already within its cause". It is held by the Vārṣagaṇya school, an early form of **Sāṃkhya**. (Master Cháng Bǎi: Vārṣa, "rain", was born in the rain; Kapila, the founder of Sāṃkhya, means "yellow-red", for his colouring.) In Sāṃkhya, everything evolves from a primordial nature that already contains it; liberation is when nature withdraws its products and stops producing.

Their four reasons: convention (people seek oil from sesame, not from sand), seeking (one looks for a result only where it is), the fixed determinacy of effort, and arising (only certain things arise from certain causes).

The treatise asks a dilemma: do cause and effect differ? If not, there is no distinction to speak of. If so, is the effect in the cause already arisen or not yet arisen? Master Cháng Bǎi's example: if curd has not yet arisen in milk, why say it is there? If it already has, why say it arises from milk?

The right view: "effect does not pre-exist within cause. Rather, there must be a cause, and, given a further condition, the effect then arises." Seeds are real potentials, but potential is not the result already existing in hiding. This matters for Yogācāra itself, which speaks of seeds "in" the ālayavijñāna.

subs.head: Five ways one thing is "in" another

blocks.text: The treatise lists five ways something can be found in another: in a location (water in a jar); in its support (eye-consciousness in the eye); through its own nature; through its activity; and through inference. None applies to an effect in its cause. Both teachers add a Yogācāra reading of the jar: "the jar stands for the ālaya, the water for the seeds". Seeds are in the ālayavijñāna in the sense of support, not as finished results.

The second doctrine, held by the same school and by the Sound-theorists, says everything already exists and conditions merely reveal it, as a light reveals a table already in a dark room. Venerable Miào Jìng warns against confusing this with the Buddhist teaching that buddha-nature is "revealed by conditions": the outsiders apply it to conditioned things, Buddhism to the unconditioned. Tomorrow's reading refutes it.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, through how many divergent doctrines is unsound reasoning attention made manifest?
quiz.why: "Unsound reasoning attention is made manifest through these sixteen distinct divergent doctrines," from effect-in-cause to false auspiciousness. Fascicle 6 reaches only the fifth, permanence; the other eleven follow in fascicle 7. A and B are totals the lectures mention, not this treatise's scheme.

quiz.q: According to Master Cháng Bǎi, there are ninety-five or ninety-six non-Buddhist schools. Why does the treatise treat only sixteen doctrines?
options: the treatise covers only south India
the ninety-odd schools reduce to sixty-two views, whose gist never goes beyond these sixteen
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Though there are ninety-five or ninety-six schools, they reduce to sixty-two views, and their gist never exceeds the sixteen doctrines." He adds: "Without careful reflection their teachings may seem partly reasonable; without wisdom one cannot refute them." Hence the treatise refutes each in detail.

quiz.q: Most of the sixteen are non-Buddhist, but Master Cháng Bǎi notes two are also held within Buddhism. Which?
options: past and future truly exist (the Sarvāstivāda) and positing a self (the Vātsīputrīya's self "neither identical to nor apart from the aggregates")
harming as Dharma and false auspiciousness
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "The Sarvāstivādin śrāvakas hold that the three times truly exist and the substance of dharmas endures"; "within Buddhism, the Vātsīputrīyas posit a self neither apart from nor identical to the aggregates." The text itself says "even those within this very teaching" for the third doctrine. (The reading note presents the self doctrine as non-Buddhist only; the lecture includes the Vātsīputrīyas.)

quiz.q: According to the treatise, which school holds that effect exists within cause?
quiz.why: "Always, at every time without exception, effect exists as a property already within its cause. It is the Vārṣagaṇya school … that holds this position." Master Cháng Bǎi: the *Cheng weishi lun* identifies it as a branch of Sāṃkhya. Venerable Miào Jìng notes his edition misprints 雨 as 兩.

quiz.q: After the refutation, how does the text state the right view of cause and effect?
options: effect does not pre-exist in cause; there must be a cause, and given conditions the effect arises
quiz.why: "Therefore, effect does not pre-exist within cause. Rather, there must be a cause, and, given a further condition, the effect then arises." Master Cháng Bǎi: "Milk still needs conditions to yield its result; the curd is not already in the milk." Venerable Miào Jìng, in Yogācāra terms: the ālaya holds the capacity to produce all dharmas, but not yet the results.

quiz.q: The text gives five marks by which one existing thing is known to be in another. What are the examples for the first two?
options: curd in milk; sprout in seed
smoke in fire; moon in water
stone in mountain; fish in sea
found in a location, like water in a jar; found in its support, like eye-consciousness in the eye
quiz.why: "First, it can be found occupying a location, as water is found within a jar. Second, it can be found within its proper support, as eye-consciousness is found within the eye." Third, through its own characteristic, not inference; fourth, through its own function; fifth, the effect changes when cause or condition changes. None is found for "effect in cause."
